That was kind of hard at that time because he started back to work and he was working in Kellogg for a while, and we were staying here. And Mom was working and Dad was working.

words: I don't know if I can get that into the camera.

words: Nobody will be on time. You can count on that. Oh, Dad was working in Kellogg. And I was going to school. I remember I'll always be thankful for hot water and I still think about that once in a while. God, I don't know how long I was going to go to haul it in a bucket anymore. words: Oh, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And we used to go,

speaker: Speaker 2

words: And she,

speaker: Speaker 2

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Chew on grain.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you ever chew on grain? Uh-uh. It's good. It's crunchy. It's just like chewing on nuts, kind of. Uh-uh. We'd steal chicken feed and the old lady Miller would get mad and change us out. words: Did he ever finish school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, he finished school, and he has about two years of college. He was going to be a farm assistant one time. That's why we moved to Coquitlam. So we got married.

words: And what were your expectations before marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Before marriage, I really don't know what I expected at the time because I kind of enjoyed after we moved into our own house that we rented, I really enjoyed doing that. speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were they really glad to have you living there?

words: Well, they didn't try and just, you know, we were already married. And I think everybody kind of suspected that I was pregnant, but nobody ever really asked. speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were, you weren't pregnant then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I wasn't pregnant. No, I didn't have Bob until about two and a half years later.

words: Did you have some kind of birth control? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just lost. Oh, I got pregnant once. I had a miscarriage at about three months, maybe about a year before Bob was born. So I did get pregnant once.

words: What kind of damage did you do to your mom?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Being married?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, a miscarriage.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Miscarriage? It was kind of shattering because I didn't know what was happening because...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You didn't know you were pregnant?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. I knew I was pregnant, but I never had a, I had talked with any women about pregnancy, and my doctor didn't really explain things to me. He just expected I should know. And he gave me this one little book, which if I look back on it now, it was like primer, first grade stuff in the respect of how I see it today, and how I feel like I understand it, with being just a little elementary. I was in the hospital for a day or so, and it was kind of a shattering thing. And then everybody, my folks came up, it seems like, they were in Kennewick then, and I'd never been in the hospital that I recall. Here I was in the hospital propped up with my feet up, upward, in a bed, and all my brothers-in-law and my mother-in-law, everybody came like it was a wake, you know. It was, that I can really recall. Here's always my mother and father-in-law and six boys standing there, you know. The oldest brother down to the littlest one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you in Kennewick at the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we didn't live there then. But they were just a very concerned family unit, that family was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I get the feeling that you liked his family quite a bit.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. I liked his family real well. I like all of the brothers individually. Now that they're married, I don't care for the family units in some respects because we have such different interests. I mean, I can, I don't, I wouldn't choose those women as my friends, probably, except the one, the oldest sister-in-law, she and I have always gotten along well, even though we have differences of opinions about a lot of things. We understand each other and respect one another for it, and we get along fine. The other ones, I just, I don't know, I can't cope with them. Some of them I'd rather not be around.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm just curious. I wanted to address your history of family, because I think that's important. Sometimes a really traumatic thing that happens. I've had different friends who've had them, and he's described it, and the way it happens sometimes is important, and it's easy to see the tragedy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was, I can recall my husband was working. He worked in a drugstore, and we didn't have a phone, and it was late in the evening, and I felt like I had to go to the bathroom. I just had a constant urge that I had to go to the bathroom, and then I started to bleed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I... Had you been in a hospital?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not really. I wasn't that far along. I don't think I was more than probably two or three months pregnant, if that. And then I passed a large blood clot, which I assumed was a blood clot, which was maybe as big as a small line or something.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Not as big as a tennis ball? Maybe.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: As big as a tennis ball? I don't know. It wasn't large. Well, it probably wasn't as bad for you as you thought that that was a blood clot. Initially, that's what I thought it was. And so I can't recall how I got to a phone. It seems like I waited until Russ got home from work, and then we went to a pay phone, and I called the doctor, and he had me go right to the hospital and meet him at the hospital. And when I told him that I'd passed from blood, he assumed I was still pregnant and that that's all it was. And then the next day he had another doctor examine me, a doctor that I didn't know from Adam's ass, you know, which... And that was kind of, well, when you're 16 or 17 or whatever, however old I was, 17, maybe 18, that was shattering because you're not used to...it's embarrassing. And I didn't know him or anything. They both assumed I was still pregnant until the next month I resumed my menstrual cycle again. Oh, my goodness. They both thought I was still pregnant.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Both thought?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because, see, my pregnancy wasn't far enough advanced. I don't think that they could really tell if my uterus had expanded, really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. And being the first patient, many others experienced... Right. Yeah. I'm interested in what you're saying about the hospital because I think a lot of times when women go to the hospital for female endocrinology, many times things aren't explained to them or...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, they just do this. So often it seems like they just do this as a matter of course. I've been reading just different articles I've read about childbirth lately and about giving drugs to the mother to ease her pain and to slow her labor or to speed up her labor for the convenience of the doctor. I think forceps and the position, you know, flat on your back, stir it with your feet in stirrups and your hands restrained and this sort of thing. And I look at it and I think that's a terrible thing. My mother-in-law had, I think, almost all of her children at home. And looking back on it, I think that's probably would be better unless you run into difficulties. I mean, if you had reason to believe that you were going to have complications, you'd want to be in the hospital. But I see absolutely no reason for PrEP. And the things I've read about that are kind of funny too. They say the reason they do this is for cleanliness, yet there's no higher incidence of infections or anything with or without the PrEP. As a matter of fact, those that have had it sometimes have abrasions from being scraped by the razor, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How was it? It's ridiculous.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And the position and then the closeness of the baby, the baby's taken away right away, wrapped up and cleaned up, you know. And forceps were used. I don't know if they needed them or not. But they say with the drugs it slows, it retards the action of your muscles so that they have to use forceps in order to deliver the baby. Well, they used forceps with every one of my children. And how was the thing was that nobody ever told you that there was another one you did? No. I mean, the doctor said so. You know, they never questioned it. And I wasn't old enough or I hadn't reached, I don't know, self-assurance enough or confidence that I questioned anything that he did. And I question now what my doctors do to me. And I've quit going to more than one doctor just because of that. If they won't explain as I want them, you know, fully enough, or if they talk down to me. I went to a doctor one time and I had this terrible, terrible sore throat. And I have this occasionally. And my own doctor was good, so I went to another doctor. He said, oh, I think you have an allergy. It must be the grass. I said, there isn't any grass at this time of the year they'd be allergic to. And he said, well, you're rubbing, you know, your nose. And this is an indication of an allergy. And he says in this length of time you've been here, you've rubbed your nose four or five times. And I said, yeah, I got a runny nose. I said, why? It's not an allergy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He said, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So he was going to examine my. He didn't even look at my throat, nose, ears, anything. He said, you have an allergy. And he gave me some medicine. He says, I'm going to prescribe this medicine for you. I said, what is it? And he says, oh, it's a little blue pill. And I said, I don't really give a damn what color the pill is. What is it? And he said, well, it isn't an antibiotic. And I got mad and I laughed. And I got home, and by the time I got home I was just serious. So I called back and asked the nurse for an appointment with my doctor. And she said, but, Donna, you were just dead. You just saw a doctor such and such. I said, I know I did. I said, that's why I want to see my own doctor. He didn't do a goddamn thing, you know. And I told my doctor, and he was angry, really angry, because he agrees that a patient shouldn't be, you know, talked down to like that. I have a pretty good understanding with that doctor, my present doctor, but he's so pressed, it seems, with his results, you know, he doesn't really have the time. You know, I can't remember from one time to the next what he's done. You know, that sort of thing. It doesn't seem like he reviews enough that he knows what you're in there for the next time you come in or what your path has been.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They are really good. Yes. Let's get back to Kyle and the reason. What factors most were you affected in the decision about how many children you wanted to have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the first one I wanted to have badly. We both wanted that child real bad. And the next one was only 15 months away, so that pretty well points to an accident. We wanted more children, but I don't think we would have actually planned on having one that quickly, because at the time my husband anticipated finishing school, pharmacy school. And then the third one, we had planned on having her, and so I stopped taking birth control pills, and then our marriage just started really sliding. And by the time we realized that, you know, that it was lost, I was pregnant. But rather than stay married, knowing that he wanted out, I got a divorce, and I had her later.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you were first married, the first two kids that we had, was there any birth control instruments you were able to use? It seems like I used,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't recall that I used any birth control device or any kind of pills between the time I had the boys. But I did after I had the second one. I don't recall if the pill was in use much at that time, and I didn't use the other. I don't know why if I never asked. I know the doctor I had here before we moved to Povertello would probably be kind of reluctant. I don't recall that I ever asked him because I was embarrassed, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, you should provide that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I know. It's something that I think is great. So, always birth control information is available. I think it's great because it will, obviously it's going to deter a lot of young, young marriages and give people a chance to become a little more mature before they get married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm just curious, what do you see as the future for your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is there anything that you want for them? That I want for them? I want for them to be independent individuals and to be their own self, to choose each of them, to choose a profession that they want, something they want to do, not something that they feel that they should go into because of social or outside pressure. Something that fulfills them, not something necessarily that will make them money but be frustrating to them later because it's a non-fulfilling job.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What do you do personally for recreation and relaxation? Where do you go? Oh, France. Visit friends. I go out with Florian.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Like to dance?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I love to dance. Really like to dance. I can go out and dance and never drink. I can but I don't. I enjoy going out and being with people. I like outdoors things. I'm not particularly athletic but I like to watch some sports. And I like to, I don't particularly like to fish but I like to get out and be out in it. I take the folks with camp out by myself sometimes and just go up in the woods by myself, which just completely blows my mother's mind. She thinks the bears are going to get me. Or even worse, a mountain man or something, you know. But I enjoy it going up and just being, just getting clear away. Just last summer, a friend of mine, another woman, got a raft for her husband. And we floated, I think, three times last year in the clear water. And I think this year we might try a river that's got a little more spunk. Oh, I just love that. I just love to swim. And in the winter I really don't like to do outside things because I don't like the cold at all. I don't like, when we went sledding this winter, I helped chaperone an Indian club party up to Winchester. We went sledding and that was fun. But mostly I just assumed stay inside in the wintertime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's what I heard. Yeah. It was warm. And I read. I knew that, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you do things in particular with your daughter? Not a lot, I guess. What do you do with a seven-year-old girl?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm trying to teach her how to embroider the other day, and that I don't think she's ready for it. She's just not quite ready for it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does she like the outdoors? Yeah. Oh, gosh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, she loves it. We were way, way up in North Fork last summer, and we were camped across the road from this packing bridge. You can't drive across this bridge, but you can pack animals across. It's a wide bridge, but it's not really wide enough for vehicles. It has these guy wires. There are these two cables on each side that go up, and as they get closer to the top, they get closer together. And it looks like it's real narrow, but it's really, with a little kid, it's just fun. You can sit on it. Well, what these kids were doing, they'd sit on this cable, and then they'd push themselves up and back up and scoot up on it. And they were clear up, down near the top of that bridge, which was much, oh, it had to have been 20, 30 feet tall. And the first time I noticed that they were doing that, she was across the top of that manhole.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, scary.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, she likes to do stuff like that. And then they just kind of bounce themselves down. She's kind of athletic. I kind of encourage her to be independent. Sometimes I think she's more of a feminist than me. We were watching something on TV the other night, and it showed the life of other children in other countries. And there were a bunch of Buddhist boys, Buddhist children going to school, and they had their saffron robes and their shade caps and everything, and all these children in school. And Karen said, where are the girls? And I hadn't noticed, but apparently only boys receive any kind of teaching in it, any kind of formal schooling in it. And she noticed, but I didn't even think about it. And once in a while she'll come up with it. She's beginning to be more independent. I called her kiddo the other day, and she says, I'm not a kiddo. So what are you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She says, I'm me.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And it would never occur to me, it wouldn't have occurred to me, to say anything like that when I was a kid. And I think this independence is really instilled in her. And I hope it's so much to her benefit if she can be that way when she's older. If you can live with yourself, anything else is extra. That's just frosting, and it's great, but first you're going to have to learn how to live with yourself. And if she's able to be self-supporting and happy with herself, and if she gets any of the other things, any other relationships that happen to come along, that she can be happy with, that's great. But I think first she's going to have to find herself. And this is me. I think I'm beginning to find myself now. And I wonder how much different things would have been had I not gotten married so early and would have had a chance to investigate myself and my own capabilities before I had a responsibility of a family. Because for the last eight years I've been supporting my family. And I really, I didn't, that's so immediate that you don't have time for these other things because your time is completely consumed with, yeah, with the everyday things.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think that's a good place to end this series. You made a really good statement at the end. Is there anything else you want to say?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not that I think of. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think there's anything else important. I think that's a good place to end, I liked your last statement there.
